In the evening we had a thunder-shower, the wind shifted to the northwest and to-day it is pleasantly cool, which is cause of great rejoicing among our men of business, who have a more full and profitable employment than they have had for many years.

An attentive observer of the condition of the country for the last thirty years, it is with no common pleasure that I assure you, never during that period has it experienced such state of sound and substantial prosperity as at the present moment, and the prospects ahead never were better.

Our city has been for some time crowded with strangers to such extent as to make it difficult to procure lodgings; the numerous large hotels and boarding houses fairly overflowing, making up cots in their parlors and sitting rooms, and colonizing their boarders in neighboring apartments.

This congregation of strangers from all parts has afforded me an opportunity to inquire into the general state of agriculture, manufactures and trade in most of the States of the Union, and here is but one story told, there is but one feeling existing, and that is UNIVERSAL belief that nothing is so much needed to insure a continuance of prosperous times as to let legislation alone-leave things as they are. You would be surprised to hear how almost every man you see from abroad expresses himself of that opinion, and how generally the politicians are condemned for beginning thus early to get up an agitation upon the Presidential question. I was very much struck with some observations of a stranger on recent occasion. The politicians, said he, are the bane of this country, they give any measures time to show their true effects. Every measure is seized upon and converted into politics with view, as they term it, to make political capital of it. Our great men cost the country more money than would pay its whole expenses. Truly, said he, the present time, all is going well. As possible as the policy of the present Administration well settled we all understand it, and no one can deny that it is in accordance with true Democratic principles.

Now, he continued, I am no Tyler man, Van Buren man, Calhoun man, Clay man, nor any man's man, but I am Democrat and always have been one. I am, however, not little disgusted with what I see going on in attempts to get up an excitement with view to gull the People.

"If the politicians would keep quiet the people might then hope for some peace and continuance of their present prosperity. I know how it is in Ohio—there we are for letting well alone, and I have no manner of doubt, it is so very true. I should like any to tell me what there is in confusing the country, from one end to the other merely for the purposes of any and all the politicians who are in search of nothing but place and power—to obtain which they care not what becomes of the public interests or welfare."

There is so much truth in what this honest Buckeye has so well said, that though you might like to publish it, and so have incorporated it into this letter. Having spoken of politics might as well advert to what is going on here among the friends of Van Buren and Calhoun, who are at dagger points. You will have seen that there have been several public movements among the latter very recently, assembling in large numbers in the Park, passing resolutions in favor of the Palmetto candidate, &c. So yesterday afternoon some two three thousand dependents and hangers on of the corporation, as the Calhoun men say, called to sustain Van Buren, and a regular row was in consequence. The resolutions, however made to order as is usual, were finally passed. It will be curious to see how all this will end. Col. Richard M. Johnson or Old Tecumseh, as he is familiarly called, is to be here in few days, and it is said, a committee is about being organized to give him suitable reception. I understand there is an organization in almost every ward of the friends of the Colonel, and know he is very popular among the masses.

Among the thinking portion of the business men of the Democracy, a great many think, with my Ohio friend, that it would be much better to let well alone. They say President Tyler is good enough President for them; that but for HIM the country would have been under ruinous rule, and God only knows where we should have been. Men—and there are not few who think the People—the People may yet speak out; and, if they should, there is every reason to believe they will show their gratitude to the man who had the moral firmness to risk all that he has suffered from reckless and corrupt politicians by strangling the serpent, in whose coils they had prepared to envelope the People. The Veto of the Bank of 1841 the People will never forget—nor will they rest satisfied until they have shown their gratitude for that high-souled act.

I place this on record for future reference and appeal, and tell the politicians, however they may laugh at it now, the feeling is abroad, and is extending itself, through which justice will be done to John Tyler.

You must have in the various accounts given of the Repeal Convention, which lately assembled here, over which Robert Tyler, Esq, ably presided. Attempts are made to diminish the effects of the measures of the friends of Repeal in this country, and, of course, of the proceedings of the recent Convention; but it should be remembered that public opinion is now no longer confined to particular countries. Steam navigation has made but one public opinion throughout Christendom, and although its effects may be despised for a while.

Sophia Lee belonged to a class of young ladies who persuade themselves that life will be to them one uninterrupted scene of pleasure, so soon as they can escape from the thraldom of the schoolroom; who look upon marriage as the end and aim of woman's existence and can conceive of no greater stigma cast upon them than the title of "spinstermaid." She had just left school, and at the age of sixteen devoted all her time, faculties and thoughts to the great object of securing a husband. A few weeks' intercourse had been the only time in which she professed to have learned that Mr. Cameron was "generous, kind, frank, warm-hearted, intellectual and refined," and this she had gathered from conversation upon the passionate, egotistical and loose sentiment of Byron, and the more sensual, as well as more musical numbers of Moore. The history of the Empress Josephine had been very remarkable. She was born in the West Indies, and had early been prophesied by an old nuness, that she should lose her first husband, be extremely unfortunate, but she should afterwards be greater than a queen. THE author heard the prophecy long before Napoleon came to the throne, from the late Countess of Gram, who was educated in the same convent with Josephine, and had repeatedly heard her mention the circumstances in early youth. This prophecy, the authenticity of which is placed in a doubt, was fulfilled in the most singular manner. Her first husband Alexander Beauharnais, a general in the army on the Rhine, had been guillotined during the reign of terror; and she herself, who was also imprisoned at the same time, was only saved from impending death by the fall of Robespierre. So strongly was the prophecy impressed on her mind that while lying in the dungeon of Conciergerie, expecting every hour to be summoned to the revolutionary tribunal, she mentioned it to her fellow prisoners; and to amuse them, named some of them as ladies of the bed chamber, in which she afterwards lived to realize one of their number.

Josephine herself narrated this extraordinary passage in her life, in the following terms, in her memoirs. —

"One morning the jailor entered the chamber where I slept, with the Duchess d'Aguillon and two other ladies, and told me he was going to take my mattress to give it to another prisoner. 'Why?' said d'Aguillon eagerly, 'will we not instantaneously obtain a better one?' 'No, no,' he replied, with a kind smile, 'she will have no need of one. For she is about to be sent to the Conciergerie, and thence, &c., the guillotine.' At these words, my companions in misfortune uttered piercing shrieks. I consoled them as well as I could; and at length, worn out with their eternal lamentations, told them that their grief was utterly unreasonable; that not only should I not die, but live to be Queen of France. 'Why then do you not name your maids of honor?' said Madame d'Aguillon, irritated at such expressions in such a moment. 'Very true,' said I, 'had not thought of that; well my dear, I make you one of them.' Upon this the tears of one of these ladies fell apace, for they never doubted I was mad. But the truth was, I was not gifted with any extraordinary courage, but internally persuaded of the truth of the oracle.

MADAME d'Aguillon soon after became unwell, and I drew her towards the window. Through the bars a little fresh air, I there perceived a poor woman who knew us, and who was making number of signs, which first I could not understand. She constantly held up her gown, robe, and seeing she had some object in view, I called out 'robe,' to which she answered 'yes.' She then lifted up a stone and put it in her lap, which she lifted up a second time; I called out 'pierre'; upon her watch she expressed the greatest joy. Perceiving that her signs were understood, joining then the stone in her robe, she eagerly imitated the motion of cutting off the neck, and immediately began to dance and express the most extraordinary joy. This singular pantomime awakened in our minds a vague hope that possibly Robespierre might be no more.

At this moment, when we were floating between hope and fear, we heard a great noise in the corridor, and the terrible voice of our jailor, who said to his dog, and giving him at the same time a kick, 'Get out, you cursed Robespierre!' That coarse phrase at once taught to us that we had nothing to fear, and that France was saved."—Alison's History of Europe.

also boiled back against its shores, so that
even Pliny could not land before the city, but
was forced to proceed to Stabiae. The beleaguered
mountain, the sulphureous air, the quivering
earth, would not let the city even so dissolute as
Pompeii gather in places of public amusement.
CONSERVATION reigned in every street, and drove
the frightened inhabitants away from their dwell-
ings. This is doubtless the reason why so few
bodies were found. Those that perished were
slaves or those who tarried till some falling col-
umn or wall blocked up their path, and the de-
scending cinders blinded their sight as they
groped about for a way of egress. Fear and
darkness (for day was turned into night,) might
have enthralled others beyond the power of NOV-
ing. And I was standing on the same pave-
ment those terror-stricken citizens stood on two
thousand years ago, and was looking on the same
mountain they gazed on with such earnest IN-
curry and fearful forebodings. Then it rocked
and swayed and thundered before the pent-up for-
ces that threatened to send it in fragments
through the heavens. Now silent and quiet it
stood on its firm base. Yet to me it had a mo-
rose and revengeful look, as if it were conscious
of the ruin at its feet.

The excavations are more extensive than I
supposed, and the effect of the clear light of the
sun and the open sky on the deserted pavements
is peculiar and solemn. A visit to it is an epi-
sode in a man's life he can never forget. An old
column or a broken wall left of once populous
city interests us. We stand and muse over the
ruined pile till it becomes eloquent with the his-
tory of the past. If one single complete temple
be found, how it increases the interest. But to
wander through the whole city standing as its in-
habitants left it in their sudden fear, increases
tenfold the vividness of the picture. The little
household things meeting you at every turn, give
speciality to the whole. As I strode from apart-
ment to apartment, I almost expected to meet
some one within the door; I felt like an intruder
as I passed into the sleeping rooms of others—as
if I were entering the private apartments of
those who were merely absent on a ride or a visit.
The scenes were familiar, and it appeared but
a short time since the eyes of those who occupied
the dwellings, rested on the same objects. In
turning the corners of the streets I would hardly
have surprised myself to have met the inhabitants
just returning and looking on me as a stranger
and an intruder. It required an effort to con-
vince myself that these streets and these dwell-
ings were thronged and occupied for the last
time nearly 1900 years ago. I assure you the
struggle was not to call up the past, but to shape
it—and when I finally stood at the gate and
gave a farewell look to the lonely city that faintly
shone in the light of the setting sun, a feeling of
indescribable sadness stole over me, and I rode
away without the wish ever to see it again. But
the view of the bay, and the careless laughing
groups we met at every step, soon restored our
spirits. The streets were filled with loungers, all
expressing in their manners and looks the Neapo-
litan maxim dolce far niente, (it is sweet to
do nothing.) You have heard of the bright eyes
and raven tresses and musical language of the
Neapolitans; but I can assure you there is none
of it here, I. G. among the lower classes. The
ONLY difference I can detect between them and
our Indians was that our wild bloods were the
more beautiful of the two. The color is the
same, the hair very like indeed, and as to the
soft, bastard Latin they speak, it is one of the
most abominable dialects I ever heard. I know
this is rather shocking to one's ideas of Italian
women; I am sure I was prepared to view them
in a favorable, nay, even poetical light; but
amid all the charms and excitements of this ro-
mantic land, I could not see otherwise. The
old women are hags, and the young women dirty,
slip-shod slatterns. Talk about "bright-eyed
Italian maids!" Among our lower classes there
are five beauties to one good-looking woman.
